hints: Look at the P to Q to R to S chain and note the order of emissions: $\beta^-$, then $\alpha$, then $\beta^-$.
Recall how proton number $Z$ and nucleon number $A$ change in each decay: $\beta^-$ gives $Z+1$ with no change in $A$, $\alpha$ gives $Z-2$ and $A-4$.
Add the three changes together to find the net change in $Z$ and the net change in $A$ from P to S, then decide what same $Z$ but different $A$ means.
walkthrough: Let nuclide P have proton number $Z$ and nucleon number $A$, written as $^{A}_{Z}P$.
First decay P to Q is $\beta^-$: a neutron changes to a proton, so $Z$ increases by 1 and $A$ is unchanged, giving $^{A}_{Z+1}Q$.
Second decay Q to R is $\alpha$: a $^{4}_{2}He$ nucleus is lost, so $Z$ decreases by 2 and $A$ decreases by 4, giving $^{A-4}_{Z-1}R$.
Third decay R to S is $\beta^-$ again: $Z$ increases by 1 and $A$ is unchanged, giving $^{A-4}_{Z}S$.
Net change from P to S is $\Delta Z = +1 -2 +1 = 0$ and $\Delta A = 0 -4 +0 = -4$.
Same $Z$ means same element, different $A$ means different isotope. This is option B.

options.A: S has nucleon number 4 less than P because of the $\alpha$ emission, so they cannot be identical.
options.B: Proton number is unchanged overall so P and S are the same element, but nucleon number falls by 4 so they are different isotopes.
options.C: The two $\beta^-$ decays each raise $Z$ by 1 and cancel the fall of 2 in $Z$ from the $\alpha$ decay, so $Z$ is unchanged.
options.D: Although mass is reduced by the $\alpha$ particle, the proton number returns to its starting value so S is not a different element.
